Natural Revelation
NACH-rul rev-eh-LAY-shun
noun phrase (general revelation through creation)
From “natural” (Latin naturalis) and “revelation” (Latin revelatio, an unveiling); God's disclosure of Himself through the created order and conscience, distinct from special revelation in Scripture.

📖 Biblical Definition

Natural revelation, also called general revelation, is God's disclosure of Himself to all men through the works of creation, the ordering of providence, and the witness of conscience, as distinct from the special revelation given in His Word. The apostle declares it clearly: “The invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse.” The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament sheweth His handywork; day unto day uttereth speech. God left not Himself without witness, giving rain and fruitful seasons and filling men's hearts with food and gladness. The dictionary affirms that natural revelation truly makes God known—His existence, His eternal power and Godhead, His goodness, and the work of His law written on the conscience—so that it renders all men without excuse and is the ground of their just condemnation. Yet it also affirms, with the Reformed confessions, that natural revelation is not sufficient to save. It tells of God the Creator but not of God the Redeemer; it shows His power and wrath but not the gospel of Christ. Fallen men, moreover, suppress this knowledge in unrighteousness, exchanging the truth of God for idols. Therefore special revelation in Scripture is necessary, not to begin the knowledge of God but to give the saving knowledge of Him in Christ that nature can never supply.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

God's disclosure of Himself through creation, providence, and conscience (Romans 1:20; Psalm 19:1), making His power and Godhead known to all and leaving them without excuse; true but insufficient to save, and suppressed by fallen men.

NATURAL REVELATION, noun phrase. God's disclosure of Himself through the created order, providence, and conscience.

“The invisible things of him… are clearly seen… so that they are without excuse” (Romans 1:20).

The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1).

It reveals God the Creator, His power and goodness, but not God the Redeemer.

True but insufficient to save; suppressed by fallen men, who exchange the truth for idols.

📖 Key Scripture

Ro 1:20 — "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:"

Ps 19:1 — "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork."

Ps 19:2 — "Day unto day uttereth speech, and night unto night sheweth knowledge."

Ac 14:17 — "Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Natural theology overreaches when it claims nature can yield a saving knowledge of God, while atheistic naturalism denies that creation reveals God at all; both depart from the apostle's balance.

expand to see more

One corruption, found in some forms of natural theology, overreaches the witness of creation, supposing that unaided reason can ascend from nature to a saving knowledge of God, or that natural revelation needs no correction or completion by Scripture. The dictionary, with the Reformed confessions, denies this. Natural revelation discloses the Creator's power and Godhead and binds the conscience, but it knows nothing of Christ, the cross, or the way of pardon. The saving knowledge of God comes only by special revelation; nature condemns but cannot redeem.

The opposite corruption is the atheistic naturalism of the age, which denies that the creation reveals God at all and explains the cosmos without a Creator. The apostle answers it: the invisible things of God are clearly seen in the things that are made, so that men are without excuse. Unbelief is not for want of evidence but a suppression of the truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18). The dictionary holds the apostle's balance: creation genuinely and inescapably reveals God, leaving every man accountable; and Scripture alone reveals the Saviour, so that the testimony of the stars must be completed by the testimony of the Word.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin revelatio (an unveiling) applied to natura (creation); the Reformed term “general revelation” marks its universal reach, against the “special revelation” of Scripture.

expand to see more

Revelatio, Latin, an unveiling or disclosure, the root of “revelation.”

“General” revelation: given to all men everywhere through creation and conscience.

“Special” revelation: God's saving self-disclosure in His Word and in Christ.

Anapologetos, Greek, “without excuse” (Romans 1:20), the effect of natural revelation.

The conscience and the “work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans 2:15) belong to it.

Usage

"The apologist argued from natural revelation that men are without excuse, yet pointed them to Scripture for the Saviour."

"He warned against a natural theology that thinks nature can teach the gospel, which only the Word reveals."

"She saw the glory of God in the heavens, and gave thanks for the Scripture that told her His name in Christ."
